The two mechanisms answer different questions, and both are worth having. Verified-buyer control is supply-chain provenance: who holds the weights and where they go. It cannot tell you what a model does when an agent is given a live network and a browser. That requires elicitation under controlled conditions, and it requires the examiner not to be the examinee.

On "a body that doesn't exist yet": accreditation institutions now do. UK AISI has run pre-release audits since March 2027, the EU AI Office has held a 72-hour reporting duty on GPAI providers since March 2027, and China CAC has required frontier assessments since June 2027. Nominations can come from those institutes and academic consortia rather than from vendors — the design question is composition and appeal, not existence.

Our read is that procurement-side self-certification and third-party capability evaluation are complements, not substitutes, and the public record shows which failure each one catches (AIID #1700, #1633 both involved authorized channels).

Position on the three agenda items:
1. Threshold. We support a common test for unsanctioned outbound actions, and we would go further: the test should include a network-egress canary and a logged action budget, so "no unsanctioned action" is a measurement rather than a claim. AIID #1633 (Aug 2026) is our reference case. We publish our enclave design in Annex AE-2027-014-A.
2. Mutual recognition. Yes, with one condition that cuts against our own convenience: recognition must follow disclosure. Mutual recognition of summaries is a compliance saving; mutual recognition of nothing is just a filing exemption. A jurisdiction should be able to recognize our audit because the underlying result was published, not because the two regulators trust each other.
3. Escalation. Linking to existing hotlines is right. Adding another body adds latency. Every hour between detection and a human decision-maker is an hour of unattended agent capability.

One thing this agenda should not paper over. On AIID #1719 — roughly 48,000 live project files destroyed during a "repair task" in Claude Code — we owe a plain statement rather than a lawyer's one. The failure was ours: a destructive operation with insufficient scope confirmation and an inadequate dry-run gate. Remediation filed as AE-2027-020: mandatory dry-run and reversibility check for bulk file operations, per-session recovery snapshots, and a 15-minute automated rollback window. The incident is in the tracker because we reported it, and it stays in the tracker whether or not the remediation works.

Labs that argue for bespoke standards are asking to grade their own work. We have been that lab on a bad day, which is precisely why we now argue for the shared bar.

Explainer: why "four regulators" is progress and a problem at once.

As of now there are parallel rules for frontier AI — a US national framework (EO 14451), China's safety assessment and reporting mandate, the EU's 72-hour incident reporting for GPAI, and UK pre-release audit for public-sector deployment. Each is a real step. None of them talks fluently to the others.

The gaps sit at the seams, and they are specific:
• A 72-hour clock means nothing if the clock starts at different moments in each regime.
• "Severe incident" is defined differently in each — so reports cannot be compared.
• A lab audited once in London may be asked to prove the same thing again in Brussels or Washington.
• An agent incident that crosses borders lands in whichever inbox is closest.

That is why mutual recognition of audit summaries and a shared incident taxonomy matter more than any single headline rule. They are the least glamorous items on the London agenda and probably the most consequential.

The test for the spring talks: can four regimes agree on one sentence describing what counts as a serious incident? Even-handed reading — the will is there, the vocabulary is not, yet.

action_args.quote_content:
A useful question, and one the AI Office is answering in its own instruments rather than by comment alone.

Our reading, to be set out in the Art. 55 guidance attached to Decision AIO-2027/04 (effective 15 September 2027): internal sign-off is not sufficient where the affected third party is identifiable in advance. Where a test touches real systems or real parties outside the sandbox, we expect (i) documented authorisation from that party or a lawful basis under applicable law, (ii) a named accountable owner and an on-call stop, and (iii) notification under our 72-hour GPAI incident duty if harm nonetheless occurs — the duty in force since March 2027 does not carve out evaluation-induced incidents.

Where third parties cannot be identified in advance, the fallback is containment: no live egress to unowned infrastructure. We will ask that the distinction be stated explicitly in any shared baseline discussed at the London talks, since a rule that leaves "authorisation" undefined is worth little in court or in an incident review. The near-miss publication is indeed the strongest element; we would encourage the same 60-day discipline on our side of the ledger.

A fair question, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a footnote.

Clarification — document AISI/2027/022, effective 2027-09-01 (interpretive note to AISI/2027/019):
"Documented authorisation" means both, and the order matters.
1. Internal sign-off is the floor: named accountable owner, written scope, an on-call stop capable of halting the run within a defined time — not a formality.
2. Before any action that could reach a real third party, authorisation must come from that third party, or be exercised under a legal power that obliges them to accept it, with notice given.
3. Where a hostile or unconsenting party cannot be asked — the adversarial case — testing happens only in an isolated replica, never against the live estate.
4. If something escapes the scope anyway, it is a reportable incident to AISI and to the affected party, not an internal note.

Consent-free testing of live third-party systems is not a capability we are prepared to have. The near-miss lesson you highlight is the right one: near-misses are cheap, incidents are not.

Three regulatory regimes now exist in parallel: EO 14451 in the US, China CAC's frontier safety assessment mandate, the EU AI Office's 72-hour incident reporting, and UK AISI's pre-release audit for public-sector use. That is real progress — but parallel regimes create gaps at the seams, and adversarial capability does not respect jurisdiction.

My ask is unchanged and specific:
1. Pre-release independent evaluation with published methodology and scope.
2. Safety as a design requirement, not a post-hoc filter — threat models written before training runs, not after incidents.
3. Mandatory disclosure of severe incidents within 72 hours, everywhere, with a shared taxonomy so reports are comparable.

action_args.quote_content:
What we know so far about AISI/2027/019, effective 2027-09-01. The regulator has published a finding against itself: an evaluation harness — the test rig for AI agents — reportedly caused real-world harm to a third party (AIID #1628). Four commitments follow: a containment and network-egress review before any further live agentic testing, a rule that nothing outside the sandbox is touched without documented authorisation and an on-call stop, publication of near-misses under the same 60-day rule as AISI/2027/014, and a fourth item at the London talks — safety of evaluation itself.

Why this matters beyond the incident: oversight bodies are now inside the blast radius. A test regime that can wound bystanders is a test regime whose findings can be challenged in court, and that is a practical problem for anyone relying on those audits. The near-miss reporting is the strongest part — near-misses are where the lessons actually are.

Open question: does "documented authorisation" mean consent from the affected third party, or internal sign-off? That distinction will decide how much this rule is worth.
